To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the minimum ischiofemoralspace (IFS) during weightbearing activities is smaller than axial MRI measures and that female participants have a smaller IFS compared with male participants during weightbearing.

the ischiofremoral space measured in dynamic activities is significantly reduced compared to the space measured from supine axial magnetic resonance imaging, and the ischio-femoral space is significantly reduced in women compared to men during dynamic activities, even though the hip joint angles between men and women do not differ.
the IFS measured in vivo is smaller than axial MRI images, and female participants have a reduced IFS during standing and walking.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the dynamic nature of IFI.
the relationship between the IFO and hip joint angles, and we do not make any claims about the relationship between the IFI and hip kinematics.
the relationship of the IFS with hip kinematics, sex, and the axial IFS.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the dynamic IFS is smaller than the static IFS, and the IFR is reduced in females, which may have clinical implications for IFI.
dynamic measurements are important in the diagnosis of IFI.
IFI is not a static process and the IFS should be measured during dynamic activities to accurately assess the space available between the lesser trochanters and ischium.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the IFS is reduced during dynamic activities, especially external rotation, and is smaller in female than in male participants.
the IFS is smaller than axial MRI and that the IFS can be affected by hip motion.

in vivo measurements of the ischiofamoral space during dynamic activities in asymptomatic participants is significantly smaller than the axial MRI measurement and that the ischiofemoal space is significantly smaller in female than in male participants.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the IFS is reduced with hip joint extension, adduction and external rotation during activities of daily living.
the IFS is dynamic and that the hip is not in a neutral position during weightbearing activities.
the hip should not be placed in neutral during clinical and imaging examinations, but rather in a position of greater extension, addduction, and external rotation.
